newsitem.title: INDIA: Legal troubles multiply for India's Rao.
newsitem.headline: Legal troubles multiply for India's Rao.

text.p: An Indian court was set on Monday to decide whether former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao could be arrested in a criminal forgery case.

The case was one of three involving the former Congress party chief scheduled to come before courts at the start of a week that analysts said could decide the future of the political leader and his party.
The Delhi High Court was set to consider Rao's request for legal protection against arrest in the seven-year-old case.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) claims Rao was part of a conspiracy in 1989 to use forged documents to defame a rival politician. Rao has not commented publicly on the case.
Last Friday, a Delhi court issued a warrant to arrest Rao. But he immediately won temporary reprieve by requesting anticipatory, or pre-emptive, bail which amounts to legal protection against arrest.

If the High Court rejects Rao's request at the hearing set for around noon (0630 GMT), he was expected to appeal to the Supreme Court, which might take up the matter later on Monday, court officials told Reuters.
If Rao were detained, he would be put in either judicial or police custody pending a hearing on the forgery case scheduled for October 14, they said.

He could be detained in New Delhi's Tihar jail, or at another site, or put under house arrest, authorities said. However, newspapers quoted some CBI officials as saying there was a reluctance to arrest the 75-year-old former prime minister, who suffers from diabetes and heart problems.
If detained, Rao, who led the government from mid-1991 until last May when his party was defeated in general polls, would be India's first ex-prime minister to be arrested on criminal charges.

Rao stepped down as Congress party leader on September 21, when a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a separate case of criminal conspiracy to cheat a businessman of $100,000. Rao has said he is innocent.

The Supreme Court was due to convene at 10:30 a.m. (0500 GMT) to consider a police request to have the hearing on the 13-year-old cheating case set for Wednesday shifted from a crowded local courtroom to a more secure location.
Rao continues to hold clout as leader of the Congress party's legislators' group in parliament, which lends key support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition.
But pressure has mounted on him to step down, and names of potential successors are circulating in the capital.

On Sunday, Rao's former finance minister, Manmohan Singh, was named to the party's main decision-making body, stirring speculation that he was being groomed to take over as head of the parliamentary group.
Singh was the driving force behind the path-breaking liberalisation programme which opened India's economy to foreign investment and trade.
The turbaned Sikh has an international reputation as a sound economist and is known for his integrity and clean image.

Another court was set to take up allegations that law-makers of the regional Jharkand Mukti Morcha party were paid $100,000 to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion which Rao's government survived by a wafer-thin margin.
Rao has been named in the case, but he has not been charged and he has denied any involvement.
